newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Trade woes see Australian deficit widen again.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Trade woes see Australian deficit widen again.

text.p: Australia's current account deficit jumped to a year high in November on the back of the worst trade performance in the last 12 months, and economists said the outlook was for continued deterioration.
Until now, the current account had receded as a concern of financial and equity markets as it moderated from the record high levels of mid-1995 in response to a cyclical trade upswing.
But a 4.9 percent fall in exports saw the November deficit come in at a seasonally adjusted A$1.923 billion, the highest level since November 1995's A$2.333 billion deficit.

"With the economy expected to recover over the course of 1997, we expect the current account deficit to continue to widen, largely on the back of the strength of imports," Bankers Trust Australia senior economist David Bassanese said.

The fall in exports, combined with the already released 1.2 percent rise in imports, saw the trade deficit blowout by A$389 million to A$394 million, the largest trade deficit since the November 1995 shortfall of A$427 billion.
Bassanese said if exports, aided by expected higher mineral prices, were able to keep pace with imports, then the current account may not pose too much of a problem in 1997.
"If that's not the case, then the current account does loom as a potential market-mover over the course of this year," he said.
The November fall in exports continued some recent weakness. Exports have fallen in four of the last eight months, and are 8.8 percent, or A$577 million, under their January '96 peak.
While a blowout in the current account was not a foregone conclusion, economists said there were warning signs emerging.
"The trend (deficit) is certainly moving wider at a time when the economy is pretty soft," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.

A key factor behind any widening would be the strength of business investment, which the government has forecast to rise by 14 percent in the year to June 30, 1997. (It has also tipped a current account deficit of A$20 billion, inferring monthly deficits of A$1.66 billion).
Rising investment is seen as leading to import growth, because Australia imports a lot of its capital requirements.
"If we do get these investment numbers realised and consumers start spending a little bit of money, we get a big rise in imports and the current account blows out again," Citibank's Koukoulas said.
"It's a little premature to say that at the moment, but precursors for some current account widening are starting to filter through already," he added.

With the net income deficit, the largest component of the overall deficit, not expected to improve in the near future, any trade deterioration will almost certainly mean a higher current account deficit, economists said.
Through the first 11 months of 1996, the net income deficit has averaged A$1.7 billion per month, and it has been larger than the current account deficit in six of those months.
Despite the fiscal tightening implemented by the government last year, the income deficit remained a medium term problem.
"I really don't think you are going to see any major improvement in the net income deficit over the next year or so," ABN Amro chief economist Susan Creighton said.
"So it will continue to be a major force driving the current account deficit at least through the next 12 months and probably quite a bit longer," she said.
